name: Carla Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, without ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential; what does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a twelve-person crew fitting out offices and shops, and this week we are setting partitions in an insurance building. My vocational trade certificate got me onto sites, but years of measuring awkward corners made me a foreperson. The laser level starts the job; I still check the line with a tape.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Tomas is a plumber, our grown children live away, and our paid house and savings cover more than six months. This job pays well and there are plenty of local contractors, though I would compare actual rates before moving. I use AI now and then to tidy an email, but it once got board quantities wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my fit-out crew the email tool is handy, but the walls still need setting out. My laser and chalk line will earn their keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The insurance office contract is sound, and my husband Tomas has a full plumbing diary. Our house is paid for and we have more than six months saved, so I can keep my plan to stop around sixty three if our figures allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would finish the third floor partitions and take the next site contract at the same rate. In the first year of this plateau I would still check board quantities on my spreadsheet, not trust the email tool with measurements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. A quieter change would give me time to train the new carpenter and sort our own retirement numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the email tool get wrong before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It once doubled the board count for a corridor because it misread a note. I caught it against the drawing before anyone ordered materials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Will your retirement date stay fixed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No date is guaranteed. Tomas and I will look at costs and our health when we get there, then decide whether another contract makes sense.

say: I would tell the **fit-out crew** that email help does not set out a wall.
I would insist on checking **board quantities** against the drawing before ordering.
think: Our **paid house** and savings leave space to keep the current retirement plan.
I still have to check **costs and health** before choosing a final work date.
do: Finish the **insurance partitions** and seek the next contract at the same rate.
Check **board quantities** on my spreadsheet throughout the first plateau year.
feel: **Calm**, with enough time to train a new carpenter and review our finances.
S0.quote: My laser and chalk line will earn their keep.
fieldNote: Carla trusts her **site measurements** after an AI quantity error on a corridor.
Her strong **household cushion** supports a conditional retirement plan, while the plateau leaves contracts steady.

steps.text: Finish insurance partitions and seek the next similarly paid contract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our contractor to show us a working site before buying a plasterboard robot. Gary, our best taper, should help judge it because the joints are his trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning screens could make my ordering quicker, but cheaper automated bids might cut our margins and overtime. Tomas could also lose plumbing calls if his customers put repairs off, so our household wages are not certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the boss for a paid demonstration on an empty floor and a proper safety plan. If the firm offers paid instruction, I would learn the robot controls with Gary, while I check whether the next contracts still pay our crew rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in front of the crew, anxious at home about two possible income cuts. Savings buy time, but they do not replace both wages indefinitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful demonstration have to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the robot to stop when a person crosses the taped work area. Then Gary and I can inspect the joints and count the rework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm will not pay for training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on the manual contracts and ask other local contractors about their rates. I will not buy a course on the promise of a job that has not been posted.

say: I would ask for a **paid site demonstration** and a safety plan before any robot purchase.
I would bring **Gary the taper** into judging the finish and rework.
think: Cheaper bids might shrink **overtime** and Tomas could lose plumbing calls.
Our **savings** give us time, though two uncertain incomes still make me anxious.
do: Request a **paid demonstration** and inspect the robot finish with Gary.
Learn **robot controls** if the firm offers paid instruction.
Check **local contract rates** before moving to another contractor.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible fall in both household incomes.
S1.quote: I will not buy a course on the promise of a job that has not been posted.
fieldNote: Her request for a demonstration is a **request**, with participation dependent on the firm offering it.
She would learn **new robot controls** only with paid instruction, and compare contract rates before a move.

steps.text: Request a paid site demonstration with a safety plan
Learn robot controls with Gary if paid instruction is offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI in 2028 cannot hang a ceiling by itself. By 2031 a capable robot might, so I would demand a live site test before it works beside anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty I could still be leading contracts, but the office bids could change quickly and squeeze our hours. The hands-on threat would reach me at sixty three, around my possible stopping point, but a lost contract could come earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take our accounts and Tomas’s plumbing bookings to an adviser this month. If the contractor cuts two consecutive months of site hours, I would apply for a posted local foreperson job at comparable pay; I would stop earlier than planned only if our income figures truly cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can absorb a short gap, but losing the last good wages before we know our retirement costs would keep me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What safety test would you require in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put the robot on a real occupied site behind a barrier and test its emergency stop. I would keep people away from moving equipment until the supervisor signs off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does reviewing figures mean you are leaving now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would keep working the current fit-out while it pays, and an earlier exit depends on the adviser showing we can cover our costs.

say: I would tell the crew that **2028 thinking AI** precedes capable site robots around 2031.
I would demand an **occupied-site safety test** before any robot works near people.
think: Contract hours might fall **before robots** reach our trade.
Savings cover a gap, but lost **late-career wages** could alter retirement.
do: Review **household accounts** and plumbing bookings with Tomas and an adviser.
Apply for a **posted local foreperson job** after two reduced months, if the pay is comparable.
Leave **earlier than planned** only if retirement income covers our costs.
feel: **Anxious** about losing site hours before retirement figures are secure.
S2.quote: I can absorb a short gap, but losing the last good wages before we know our retirement costs would keep me awake.
fieldNote: Carla separates a **2028 planning shock** from the 2031 hands-on robot risk.
Her actual alternatives have **explicit conditions**, rather than claiming a guaranteed early exit without adequate household money.

steps.text: Apply for a posted comparable-pay foreperson job after two reduced months
Retire before sixty three only if income covers household costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our contractor that five years is enough to run a serious test on a real floor. I would want Gary and the safety lead present before a robot takes any plasterboard work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty three when thinking AI arrives and sixty six when capable site robots follow. I hope to have finished regular site work by then, provided the house and our savings still cover us; Tomas’s plumbing work may last longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would finish the insurance floor and ask the boss for paid instruction if the new planning software is adopted. If I am still employed in the first year after 2031, I would use the software on one contract and check its quantities against my drawings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for Gary, but steadier about my own finances. Five years lets me see real orders and retirement costs instead of guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take the planning course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the firm pays for it and gives me time off site to practise on a real contract. I will not promise a result from a course that has not been offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you have already left before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would review our household spending with Tomas, not turn up on a crew that no longer employs me. I could still answer Gary’s questions if he called.

say: I would ask for a **real floor trial** with Gary and the safety lead present.
I would tell the crew **thinking AI** arrives years before capable building robots.
think: I may have ended **site work** before 2031 if our savings and house costs allow.
Tomas’s **plumbing income** could still change during the longer transition.
do: Finish the **insurance floor** and request paid instruction if software is adopted.
Use new **planning software** after 2031 only if I remain employed and receive paid practice.
feel: **Uneasy** for Gary, with time to examine orders and retirement costs.
S3.quote: I will not promise a result from a course that has not been offered.
fieldNote: Her steady approach needs **paid practice** and a real contract before adopting planning software.
She distinguishes **2026 employment** from conditional work after 2031, when she may already have retired.

steps.text: Finish the insurance floor on the current crew
Learn planning software if employed and offered paid practice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a decade should be used to teach sound setting out, not just how to touch a screen. Site robots around 2039 still need a proven barrier and emergency stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty eight in 2036 I expect to be out of regular fit-outs if our income and health allow it. Robots arrive near seventy one for me, so my main concern is whether Gary and the younger carpenters still get paid practical training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, in 2026, I would teach the apprentice to read a ceiling drawing and mark the first partition with me. In the first year after 2036, if retired, I would check our household income and perhaps visit a trade class; if still employed, I would use only site equipment approved by the safety lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own timing, concerned for the trade. A good wall starts with someone who knows what the drawing leaves out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the apprentice practise first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She would set out a crooked corner with the laser, then check it with a tape and square. I would have her explain why the board cut changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you work until the 2039 robot date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if our income required it, my health allowed it and a contractor still paid for my work. I have no reason to make that date a retirement target.

say: I would urge **paid site teaching** through the long transition.
I would require **barriers and emergency stops** before 2039 robots work near people.
think: I expect to leave regular fit-outs before **2036**, if our income permits.
Younger carpenters need **paid practical training** to keep their route into the trade.
do: Teach the **apprentice** drawing and partition checks now in 2026.
Review **household income** after 2036 if retired; work only if still employed and safe.
feel: **Calm** about my own plan, with concern for younger workers.
S4.quote: A good wall starts with someone who knows what the drawing leaves out.
fieldNote: Her own expected **retirement** precedes the AGI and robot dates, conditional on income and health.
She specifies separate **2026 teaching** and conditional activity after 2036.

steps.text: Teach the apprentice drawing and partition checks in 2026

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a lost fit-out contract could cut my last strong earning years before site robots arrive. Clear hours and contract forecasts, a paid safety trial, and honest retirement figures would let Tomas and me decide what we can afford.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: What should I have asked about?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets to inspect the finished joints when a robot does the plasterboard. Gary, our best plasterboard taper, can spot a poor finish from across the room.

headlineQuote: Gary, our best plasterboard taper, can spot a poor finish from across the room.
portrait: **Carla**, 58, leads office and shop fit-outs after earning a vocational trade certificate and years of site experience.
She has **higher pay**, a paid house, over six months of savings and many nearby contractors, while Tomas earns plumbing income.
Her **steady approach** asks for real site evidence, paid instruction and clear safety controls before adopting unfamiliar equipment.
She plans a **conditional retirement** around sixty three, and fears lost contract hours before then more than the robot itself.
biggestWorry: A **2028 contract shock** could cut Carla’s last strong earning years before capable site robots arrive.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **contract hours**, paid trials and reliable household retirement figures would help Carla choose her next step.
